title: NOCTI Biotechnology 4275: Knowledge of Biotechnology - Biotechnology - Food processing
subject: Biotechnology

questions.q: For centuries, cheese manufacturing required the slaughter of unweaned calves to extract the milk-curdling enzyme rennet from their stomachs. Today, over $90\%$ of commercial hard cheeses are made using a recombinant enzyme produced by genetically modified bacteria and fungi (such as *Aspergillus niger*). What is the name of this biotechnologically produced enzyme?
questions.explain:
The active curdling enzyme historically found in calf stomachs is **chymosin**. 

Biotechnologists isolated the cow gene for chymosin and inserted it into microorganisms to create **Fermentation-Produced Chymosin (FPC)**. In 1990, FPC became the very first artificially produced recombinant enzyme approved by the FDA for use in food. This advancement stabilized the global cheese supply chain and allows for strictly vegetarian cheeses. 
> *Lactase* (Option 'd') breaks down milk sugars (lactose), but does not curdle proteins for cheese.

questions.q: During the industrial production of yogurt and sauerkraut, wild or engineered strains of Lactic Acid Bacteria (LAB) undergo strictly anaerobic fermentation. Biochemically, how does this fermentation process inherently preserve the food and prevent the growth of deadly spoilage organisms like *Clostridium botulinum*?
options: The bacteria secrete broad-spectrum penicillin that destroys the cell walls of competing microbes.
The bacteria rapidly metabolize free sugars into lactic acid, drastically dropping the pH of the food into an acidic, inhospitable range.
The bacteria perform oxidative phosphorylation to boil the water out of the food matrix, creating a dry, desiccated environment.
The bacteria bind all the free nitrogen gas in the food, starving spoilage organisms of vital atmospheric nutrients.
questions.explain:
Food preservation via fermentation works primarily through **acidification**. 

Under anaerobic conditions, Lactic Acid Bacteria (like *Lactobacillus* species) convert simple carbohydrates into **lactic acid** as a metabolic waste product. This rapid accumulation of acid drastically lowers the pH of the food environment (usually below $4.6$). Highly pathogenic and spoilage microbes (especially *C. botulinum* spores) cannot survive or germinate in high-acid environments, rendering the fermented food safe and shelf-stable.
